# Wiki Page Ids

Some page types allocate short ids that other pages cite. This lookup holds how those ids are allocated, how a citation names one, and what happens to them when content moves between pages.

**See also:** `wiki-authoring-spec` — for the readability rules and the list of every author-facing lookup.

## Row and criterion ids

Some page types allocate short ids their siblings cite across pages: a `feature`'s or a
`task-flow`'s `AC<n>` acceptance criteria, a `test-scenario`'s `TS<n>` scenario rows, and a
`task-flow`'s `S<n>` steps, `A<n>` and `E<n>` alternate and error paths, and `T<n>` anytime
actions. Ids are **page-local** — identity is the composite of the page and the id, which is what
a citation like `@verifies <subject>#TS1` already carries, so a globally-unique id would restate
the namespace the citation supplies and let the halves drift.

Allocate monotonically and never reuse. The next id is one past the highest ever issued on that
page, not one past the current count: on a page that has issued `AC1` through `AC4`, deleting
`AC3` leaves a hole and the next criterion is `AC5`. Renumbering is the same defect seen from the
other side — it silently repoints a citation at a criterion it was never written against, which
reads as coverage while asserting something the test does not check. A hole costs a reader
nothing; a reused number costs them the traceability the id existed for. Each prefix is its own
sequence. Where the ids label an ordered list — a flow's steps — the list's order is the reading
order, not the ids': on a flow that has issued `S1` through `S4`, a step inserted after `S2` is
`S5`, placed where it runs.

A `test-scenario` row names the criteria it verifies in its `Verifies` cell, comma-separated and
in plain text — an id in inline code is an example and one in a comment is a note, neither a
citation. **A citation is authorized by the page's subject:** a bare id names a criterion of that
subject, and a qualified form names another page, which is legal only from a page whose subject is
a flow that page is linked with. So the form follows from the subject, not from the tier — one
grammar at every tier rather than one per tier.

- `AC<n>` — a criterion of the page's own subject, whichever kind its `tier` admits. A subject
  that declares no `## Acceptance criteria` has none to name, so a bare id on such a page cites
  nothing; only `feature` and `task-flow` declare criteria.
- `<module>/<feature-slug>#AC<n>` — a criterion of a feature that is NOT the page's subject, named
  by its path with `features/` dropped. The page's subject must be a flow the feature lists under
  `## Task flows`. A criterion of the page's own feature subject takes the bare form instead: an
  `e2e` page proving a criterion that spans its feature's flows cites it as `AC<n>`.
- `flows/_shared/<task>#AC<n>` — a criterion of the shared base the page's flow specializes,
  qualified by its page path; the `flows/` prefix keeps it from reading as a feature path. A base
  only one deliverable's areas share sits under that deliverable and is cited the same way, by its
  path: `flows/<deliverable>/_shared/<task>#AC<n>`. The page's subject must be a flow that links
  that base under `## Delta from the shared flow`. The base's criteria are covered on the base's
  own `test-scenario`; a specializing row cites one to record that the criterion holds for the
  specialization too.
- `—` — none.

`## Out of scope / other tiers` names a criterion verified at another tier with the same tokens.


## Splitting and merging

Both operations move content between pages, so both move the ids that content carries, and
both are relocations rather than retirements wherever a page survives.

**Splitting.** Create the new page, move the content into it, then relocate anything that
changed path with the wiki's move step, which repoints every citation of the moved page across the
wiki and the code tree. What the move step cannot do is decide which half a criterion belongs
to — that is the authoring judgment the split exists to make.

**Merging.** Move the content into the surviving page first, then retire the emptied one by
archiving it into the survivor, naming the survivor's `<domain>:<path>`, so the stub forwards a reader to
the live page rather than to the frozen pre-merge copy. Never leave the emptied page in place
as a near-duplicate.

**Ids that move with their content.** Identity is the composite of the page and the id, which
is what a citation like `@verifies <subject>#TS1` already carries — so a row or criterion that
moves to another page **keeps its number and changes its page half**. The source page keeps a
hole at that number, exactly as a deletion leaves one, and the destination allocates above its
own highest-ever issued id for that prefix. Re-issuing a moved criterion from `AC1` on arrival
is the defect this file already names: it silently repoints a citation at a criterion it was
never written against. Every `Verifies` cell and every code citation naming the old page and id
has to name the new page and the same id.

**A `test-scenario` names exactly one subject.** Splitting a `feature` or a `task-flow`
therefore forces a matching split of the `test-scenario` pages that verify it; the `TS<n>` rows
follow the same keep-the-number rule.
